To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
irradiation produces changes in gastric mucus output that may compromise the ability of gastric mocus to protect the gastric mucosa.

irradiation increases both acidic glycoprotein and neutral glycoprotein outputs during basal secretion, abolishes postprandial acidic glycoprotein output, decreases chloride and fluid outputs, and has no effect on sodium or potassium ion outputs.
ionizing radiation causes significant changes in both gastric mucus quantity and nature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of ionizing radiation on the gastrointestinal tract.
the effect of radiation on gastric mucosal integrity and the protective role of the gastric mucus barrier.
the effect of ionizing radiation on the gastric mucosa of the rhesus monkey.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of radiation on gastric mucus secretion were not only dose-related, but also time-related, and that the changes were not due to the effects of radiation per se on mucus secretion, but rather due to the changes in the blood circulation and the changes in the gastric mucosal microenvironment.
ionizing irradiation produces significant alterations in gastric mucus output.
irradiation produces a profound alteration in gastric mucus glycoprotein secretion in the rhesus monkey.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ionizing irradiation produces significant alterations in the quantity and composition of gastric mucus glycoprotein secreted into the stomach.
ionizing irradiation alters the quantity and nature (composition) of soluble mucus secretions.
radiation exposure results in a decrease in gastric mucus output and an alteration in the composition of the mucus glycoprotein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiation exposure causes significant alterations in the quantity and nature (acidic vs. neutral) of gastric mucus secreted into the stomach.
ionizing irradiation produces significant alterations in both the quantity of soluble gastric mucus glycoprotein and the nature of the glycoprotein secreted into the juice.
radiation exposure causes changes in the composition of the mucus layer, which may have implications for radiation-induced gastrointestinal damage.
